title: Cereal crops supplied predominantly by biological nitrogen fixation

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a cereal crop–microbe system that obtains most of the crop’s nitrogen from atmospheric nitrogen, while maintaining competitive yield and grain quality without synthetic nitrogen fertilizer. Nitrogen-fixing microorganisms would convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms the crop can use and transfer enough of it to support growth as demand changes through the season. The defining advance is dependable, predominant nitrogen supply under ordinary farming conditions, beyond a small supplemental contribution.

Root nodules are one possible biological route, but they are not a requirement for this concept. The supplied study investigates genetically edited bacteria associated with maize roots, providing a relevant route to nitrogen fixation and transfer without making nodulation the definition of success. Maize supplies the documented example; extending the capability to wheat, rice or other cereals remains prospective.

significance.text: If biological fixation reliably supplied most cereal nitrogen, the direct consequence would be substantially reduced dependence on manufactured nitrogen fertilizer wherever the system worked. Achieving this while preserving crop productivity would change a major recurring input requirement for staple farming. The supplied maize study establishes a relevant partial contribution, but does not demonstrate this larger transformation.

Reduced fertilizer manufacture could lower associated energy use and greenhouse-gas emissions. Better alignment between nitrogen supply and crop demand could also reduce nitrate leaching and nitrous-oxide emissions. These environmental benefits remain conditional: their size would depend on actual fertilizer displacement, the biological system’s resource requirements, nitrogen losses and farm management. The paper describes potential reductions in field losses while explicitly calling for research to confirm and quantify them.

As a synthesis of the proposed capability, this would address the nitrogen-supply component of cereal production, rather than establish general independence from agricultural inputs. Success in maize would not by itself establish equivalent performance in wheat or rice, and predominant biological supply would not mean that every unit of crop nitrogen came from the atmosphere. Claims about broader farm economics or environmental transformation would require measurements beyond nitrogen delivery alone.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability still to be demonstrated within the supplied evidence is reliable, high-output fixation and transfer that supplies most cereal nitrogen in step with crop demand. Fixation alone is insufficient: nitrogen must reach the plant in useful quantities at the right times without compromising yield or grain quality. The 2024 study demonstrates partial provision rather than this full capability; the supplied record cannot establish whether the broader goal remained unmet across the field as of November 1, 2026.

A concrete biological barrier is nitrogenase’s vulnerability to oxygen damage. Field performance also varies with moisture, temperature, soil pH and carbon availability. Engineering a useful system therefore requires maintaining microbial activity and nitrogen transfer across changing root environments and management conditions, while matching the timing and magnitude of crop nitrogen demand. A result under favorable experimental conditions does not establish that robustness.

An additional engineering question is how the biological system’s energy and carbon requirements affect crop performance at much higher nitrogen-delivery rates. The earlier research identified energy consumption as a barrier, but the supplied review did not find direct substantiation of that separate assertion in the reviewed text. It is therefore retained here as an unresolved resource-budget question, without assigning a quantified cost or treating it as an established explanation for the observed field result.

Measurement is also a barrier to convincing demonstration. Estimates of atmospheric-derived nitrogen in cereals can carry substantial uncertainty, and improved recovery of fertilizer nitrogen can resemble part of the isotope signal attributed to fixation. Establishing predominant biological supply requires separating newly fixed nitrogen from fertilizer uptake and soil nitrogen, rather than inferring the mechanism from crop growth or an isotope shift alone.

current_state.text: Martinez-Feria, Simmonds and colleagues’ 2024 Scientific Reports paper reports partial nitrogen provision to maize by genetically edited root-associated bacteria. The reviewed account distinguishes two forms of evidence: transfer of labeled atmospheric nitrogen to maize was demonstrated under controlled conditions, whereas the reported field quantity was inferred using nitrogen-isotope natural-abundance measurements and isotope dilution. The controlled transfer demonstration should not be presented as direct labeled-gas tracing of the field contribution.

In the study’s 2022 multisite field trials, the estimated average contribution from PROVEN 40 was 21.2 kg nitrogen per hectare to maize aboveground biomass by the VT–R1 growth stages, approximately 11% of that biomass’s nitrogen. The reported 95% confidence interval was −0.16 to 42.6 kg nitrogen per hectare. This preserves the useful scale of the reported contribution while showing its substantial uncertainty; it is not a precise, independently confirmed quantity or a demonstration of predominant supply.

The authors acknowledge that greater fertilizer-recovery efficiency could partly explain the observed decrease in the nitrogen-isotope signal, potentially inflating the estimated contribution attributed to fixation. The confidence interval includes zero, so this estimate alone does not precisely establish a positive field contribution at the reported confidence level. Neither that uncertainty nor the alternative explanation proves that biological transfer did not occur. Authors affiliated with Pivot Bio declared competing financial interests involving the developer, patents and commercialization of the studied strains; this disclosure matters for evaluating the evidence but does not itself invalidate the experiments.

The supplied review relied on the complete 18-page main article’s prose, methods and captions. Referenced supplements and figure images were not supplied for inspection, limiting assessment of details available only in those materials. The source index records retrieval of the paper on November 11, 2026, but retrieval of a 2024 article does not establish subsequent scientific progress. With no supplied freshness record, the evidence supports a dated account of this study rather than a comprehensive assessment through November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent, multiyear farm trials across major cereal-growing regions should show that biological fixation supplies most crop nitrogen without synthetic nitrogen fertilizer, while maintaining competitive yield and grain quality. A protocol should define “most,” the relevant yield and quality comparisons, and the required regional coverage before trials begin. These are proposed completion criteria, not established standards or requirements already met by the supplied study.
completion_criteria.label: Predominant fixation sustains competitive crops without synthetic nitrogen fertilizer

completion_criteria.text: Proposed attribution requirements should combine appropriately designed isotope measurements with whole-system nitrogen balances and explicit uncertainty analysis. Trials should distinguish atmospheric nitrogen from fertilizer recovery and soil nitrogen, and test whether performance is sustained without mining soil nitrogen reserves over successive seasons. The paper’s discussion of uncertainty across natural-abundance, enrichment-dilution and nitrogen-balance methods supports using complementary evidence; simply including several methods would not guarantee valid attribution.
completion_criteria.label: Atmospheric nitrogen attribution quantifies uncertainty and tests soil nitrogen depletion

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical validation should measure nitrogen losses, greenhouse-gas emissions, whole-system resource use and cost alongside crop performance. Independent teams should reproduce the outcome, with enough methodological detail to evaluate attribution and uncertainty. Results should identify the crops, soils, climates and management conditions under which the system succeeds or fails. Finite trials could establish demonstrated breadth and useful operating boundaries, but could not establish literal universality across cereal farming.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication reports full system impacts, costs, and operating boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AGR-02, “A transferable carbon-concentrating system for C3 staple crops,” concerns carbon acquisition, while AGR-01 concerns nitrogen supply. Both seek improvements in staple-crop physiology, but neither capability establishes the other. AGR-09, “Food crops that reliably build durable, additional soil carbon,” overlaps through crop–soil processes and environmental assessment; nitrogen provision does not itself demonstrate durable, additional carbon storage.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-03, “Reliable clonal seed reproduction across major hybrid crops,” addresses reproduction and propagation, and AGR-04, “High-yield perennial versions of the major grain-crop portfolio,” addresses crop life history and sustained grain production. Nitrogen-fixing systems could potentially be combined with either, but predominant biological nitrogen supply would not demonstrate clonal seed reproduction or productive perennial cereals.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-05, “Productive staple farming with seawater and a closed salt balance,” addresses salinity and salt management, while AGR-06, “Rapidly programmable, durable crop immunity,” addresses disease resistance. Their overlap with AGR-01 is the broader aim of dependable crop performance under practical constraints. Nitrogen provision cannot substitute for either salt balance or durable immunity.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-07, “A general, rapid method for creating productive crops from wild plants,” concerns crop development and domestication; AGR-08, “Economically accessible, end-to-end autonomous field farming,” concerns farm operations and economics. They could provide settings in which biological nitrogen supply is deployed, but faster crop creation and autonomous farming remain distinct capabilities with separate completion criteria.

change_log.change: Preserved AGR-01’s identity and predominant-supply ambition while distinguishing the hypothetical capability from the documented partial maize result.
change_log.reason: Evidence for a smaller contribution provides a technical basis without establishing that the proposed innovation has been achieved.

change_log.change: Separated controlled labeled-atmospheric-nitrogen transfer from field estimates based on natural-abundance isotope measurements.
change_log.reason: The earlier description of isotope-tracer field experiments conflated different experimental settings and attribution methods.

change_log.change: Specified the 2022 field-trial date, 2024 publication, aboveground-biomass scope, VT–R1 timing, 21.2 kg nitrogen per hectare estimate, approximately 11% contribution and 95% confidence interval.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the result’s quantitative value while preventing an overly precise or whole-season interpretation.

change_log.change: Integrated improved fertilizer recovery as an alternative contributor to the isotope signal and explained the interval’s inclusion of zero.
change_log.reason: Both materially qualify field attribution without proving that biological nitrogen transfer was absent.

change_log.change: Retained oxygen sensitivity, environmental variability, synchronization and the distinction between nodulation and root-associated bacterial routes.
change_log.reason: These scientific distinctions explain the engineering challenge and prevent an unnecessarily narrow definition of success.

change_log.change: Recast the energy-consumption assertion as an unresolved resource-budget question.
change_log.reason: The review did not find direct support for that separate assertion in the supplied text; retaining it with qualification preserves the question without inventing evidence.

change_log.change: Kept environmental benefits conditional and made proposed completion criteria explicitly prospective.
change_log.reason: Reduced emissions and pollution require lifecycle and field measurements, while the proposed demonstration thresholds are not established standards.

change_log.change: Added financial-interest disclosures, review-access limitations and the absence of evidence establishing subsequent progress.
change_log.reason: Readers need these boundaries to interpret the dated study without treating conflicts as disproof or source retrieval as a current literature assessment.

change_log.change: Explained connections and distinctions with all eight other roster entries.
change_log.reason: The concepts share agricultural aims but represent separate capabilities and should remain separate records.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish progress after the 2024 publication or whether predominant biological nitrogen supply remained unmet across cereal systems as of November 1, 2026.
The share of the field isotope signal attributable to fixation rather than improved fertilizer recovery remains uncertain.
The supplied material does not establish independent replication of the reported field quantity or predominant supply in wheat, rice or other cereals.
Referenced supplements and figure images were unavailable to the supplied review; details confined to those materials remain unassessed.
The resource costs of substantially higher fixation and transfer, and their effects on crop performance, remain unresolved in this record.
A future demonstration protocol must operationalize predominant supply, competitive yield and grain quality, regional coverage, uncertainty requirements and acceptable practical boundaries.
Net effects on nitrogen losses, greenhouse-gas emissions, long-term soil nitrogen and farm cost require direct measurement.

brief.title: Grain crops that get most of their nitrogen from air
possible: Farmers could grow grain crops without synthetic nitrogen fertilizer while maintaining competitive harvests and grain quality. Microbes living with the crop would convert nitrogen from the air into nutrients and supply most of what the plants need throughout the season.
why: For staple-crop farmers, this would greatly reduce dependence on a major recurring input. Replacing manufactured nitrogen fertilizer could also cut the energy use and greenhouse-gas emissions associated with making it.
Supplying nitrogen closer to where and when plants need it could reduce nitrogen pollution in water and emissions from fields.

sources.who: Rafael Martinez-Feria, Maegen B. Simmonds and colleagues
sources.showed: Gene-edited root bacteria supplied nitrogen to maize under controlled conditions. This demonstrated biological nitrogen fixation (BNF): microbes converting nitrogen from air into plant nutrients. Field experiments estimated a partial contribution.
sources.quote:
BNF is demonstrated in controlled 
environments by the transfer of labeled 15N2 gas from the rhizosphere to the chlorophyll of inoculated 
maize plants.
sources.cited_for: Edited bacteria can fix atmospheric nitrogen and transfer it to maize.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish dependable supply of most crop nitrogen without synthetic fertilizer.

sources.who: Layne N. Connolly and colleagues at Ohio State University
sources.showed: Field experiments with traditional maize varieties estimated partial nitrogen supply from air. Estimates varied with the variety, fertilizer use and comparison plant.
sources.quote: Up to 36% of plant N was derived from the atmosphere, with values varying by accession, the reference plant used, and the fertilizer level.
sources.cited_for: Traditional maize varieties offer another route to obtaining atmospheric nitrogen.
sources.not_established: The trials do not demonstrate predominant atmospheric nitrogen supply with competitive yield and grain quality.

shown: Martinez-Feria, Simmonds and colleagues estimated that their bacteria supplied about 11% of nitrogen in maize's aboveground growth in field trials. The uncertainty included no contribution, and better fertilizer uptake could partly explain the signal. Direct transfer from air to plants was demonstrated under controlled conditions.
missing: Dependable delivery of most crop nitrogen throughout the season, without synthetic nitrogen fertilizer or reduced yield and grain quality.
Reliable microbial activity and nitrogen transfer across changing soils, weather and farm management.
Clear separation of newly fixed nitrogen from fertilizer uptake and depletion of soil nitrogen reserves.
Independent replication with measurements of nitrogen losses, emissions, resource use and farm costs.

milestones.label: Most nitrogen comes from air without sacrificing harvests
milestones.explanation: Independent farm trials over multiple years and major growing regions would have to meet predefined supply, yield and quality targets without synthetic nitrogen fertilizer. This would establish dependable predominant supply.

milestones.label: Nitrogen accounting confirms the source and protects soil reserves
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to combine measurements of distinct nitrogen forms with whole-system nitrogen accounting and explicit uncertainty across seasons. This would distinguish atmospheric supply from fertilizer uptake and soil depletion.

milestones.label: Independent trials establish impacts, costs and limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce crop performance and measure nitrogen losses, emissions, resource use and costs across farming conditions. This would establish practical benefits and where the system succeeds or fails.

uncertain: The energy and carbon needed for much higher nitrogen delivery could affect crop performance.
Success in maize would not establish equivalent performance in wheat, rice or other cereals.
Trials still need agreed definitions of predominant supply, competitive harvests, grain quality and sufficient regional coverage.
